doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Growing to appreciate Bill Evans and Ornette Coleman
summary: He recalls disliking Bill Evans's Village Vanguard record in 1963, then suddenly understanding it, and a similar delayed understanding of Ornette Coleman.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: For instance, the first time I heard — I was a senior in high school in Germany and I went down to the PX and bought this record Bill Evans “Sunday Live at the Village Vanguard.” I brought that back home, Scott LaFaro, Paul Motian. Put it on, now Bill Evans for me was this guy who used to play with Miles back in the late fifties and he’s on a couple of Miles’ records and so and I remember he also used to play with people like Jimmy Giuffre, Tony Scott, there were some — I remember that. But I never had any of those records. I just remember hearing a couple of things and kind of enjoying it and sort of west coastish but no not really, but — because I never listened to anything but his Bud Powell roots which is where Bill Evans really came out of anyway. But so I buy this record, put it on and start playing. I guess the first tune is “Gloria’s Step” and then it goes on from there, various tunes and whatever is on the record. But “Alice in Wonderland” and all sorts of other things. And I’m saying to myself what’s wrong — because I’m thinking Wynton Kelly and Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb or Philly Joe and Wynton Kelly and Paul Chambers and Percy Heath playing with Mickey Roker, all this king of thing, Ray Brown with Kenny Clarke and John Lewis and Milt Jackson and stuff. And here’s these guys playing [scats] and they get into musical conversation. Man these guys don’t swing. What’s wrong with these guys. This is some sad — boy to pay two dollars and thirty-five cents for this LP in the PX — a brand new LP bought in 1963 you know. I got robbed. But now we lived about 60 or 70 miles away — about 120, 130 kilometers away from Nuremberg. So we had to go in on Sunday nights and stay in the dorm all week and then Friday night we’d get on the bus and go back home for the weekend. So I was a senior in high school, it was my last year in high school. So about two months later I walk in the house on a Friday night and something tells me go get that record, go get that record. And I’m going oh man, so sad. I put it on and it’s like whoa, hmmm. Suddenly it made all the sense in the world. Obviously I’d been thinking about it subconsciously, unconsciously. Ornette Coleman was the same way. It took me a little longer for Ornette, but the first record I bought from Ornette, I can’t remember which one it was but I’d have to look in my library because it’s a European pressing of that record. And I put that on and I didn’t get back to that for a couple of years. I didn’t understand what that was all about. And then one day I put one of Ornette’s — it wasn’t that record it was another record somewhere, and I put that on and said oh man, whoa, where have I been? Because it is, it’s gorgeous once you really understand it. It’s not about all this traditional kind of,

like what I did a clinic on today. It’s rooted in the melodies and the rhythms, but the rhythms are not supposed to be as hard and fast and they’re not supposed to be as repetitive as some of the other kinds of traditional kinds of music are. And when you finally begin to understand the emotional depth as well as the difference in approach for articulation, the difference in approach for harmonic development, the difference of approach in terms of how you block out your phrases, the kind of phrasing that you use is definitely jazz. I mean Ornette Coleman is Charlie Parker. There’s no question, Charlie Parker might have played what Ornette plays, if Charlie Parker had continued to move on and I mean — the self destruction that Charlie Parker might have been, might be similar to Trane’s self destruction in terms of the increasing harmonic and technical development that both of them obviously were moving along because they were continuing their careers, which goes in two directions simultaneously. It goes towards increasing complexity on the one hand and goes to increasing simplicity simultaneously, almost in a Zen kind of response.
